entities.summary:
Bek (fl. c. 1353–1336 BCE) served as the chief sculptor to Pharaoh Akhenaten during the revolutionary Amarna Period of Egypt's New Kingdom. Emerging from a lineage of artists—his father Men was also a chief sculptor under Amenhotep III—Bek was instrumental in manifesting the radical new artistic style that mirrored Akhenaten's monotheistic devotion to the Aten, the sun disk. His significance lies in his direct role in shaping an aesthetic that broke centuries of established artistic conventions, making him a pivotal figure in the history of ancient Egyptian art and religious expression.

Bek's primary contribution was the execution and supervision of monumental sculptures and reliefs that defined the Amarna style. This new aesthetic departed dramatically from the idealized, rigid forms of traditional Egyptian art, embracing a more naturalistic, elongated, and sometimes caricatured depiction of the royal family. Key works attributed to or overseen by Bek include the colossal statues of Akhenaten from Karnak and the distinctive portraiture found in the newly established capital of Akhetaten (modern Amarna). He explicitly states in an inscription that he was 'the apprentice whom His Majesty himself taught,' underscoring his personal connection to Akhenaten's artistic vision and the pharaoh's direct involvement in the stylistic revolution.
